records.name: Zonguldak
records.current_summary: No trans-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern is documented for this province. That absence records the absence of documented divergence — not local safety: the province remains governed by the same blanket national rules documented below.  Those rules: a judicial package leaked in October 2025 would criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality (up to three years) and same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies (up to four); raise the minimum age for gender-affirming healthcare from 18 to 25 behind a permanent-infertility mandate with state-hospital evaluations; and expose patients (up to three years) and providers (up to seven) to charges — protested by 15 LGBTI groups and the national medical association, against regional-court precedent. The country's longest-running LGBTI monitor's 2025 report finds hostility become explicit state policy: 'family' directives, the first closure of an LGBTI organisation in years, 6 right-to-life violations (3 hate-motivated killings), 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, 313 liberty violations with 299 detention decisions, and expression violations rising from 216 to 540. In July 2025 police ran mass identity-check roundups detaining trans women, recording names and images without stated legal grounds.

sources.claim: National-framework source (applies country-wide; no provincial breakdown): HRW news release, Oct 29, 2025, reports the leaked omnibus draft ("11th Judicial Package") that would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" (up to three years in prison) and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies (up to four years), and would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25 behind mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals; healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison and patients up to three years, with possible pretrial detention. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft; HRW warns it would force treatment underground and leave LGBT people in constant fear of arrest.

National-framework monitoring report (applies country-wide; no provincial breakdown): Kaos GL's 2025 review ("The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People") finds hostility toward LGBTI+ people became explicit state policy — "Year of the Family" instructions issued to public institutions and the closure of an LGBTI+ rights organisation for the first time in years, with expression and artistic freedom restricted and events cancelled or banned. It documents 6 right-to-life violations including 3 hate-motivated killings (trans people the most affected), 89 torture/ill-treatment violations (up from 51 the prior year), 313 liberty violations — about two and a half times the previous year — with 299 detention decisions, private-life violations rising from 16 to 67 including obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy, and 61 travel bans.

records.name: Antioquia
records.current_summary: Antioquia contains the city at the centre of the country's most alarming recent record on anti-trans killings. On 4 April 2025 in Bello, a 32-year-old trans woman, Sara Millerey González Borja, was beaten and thrown into a waterway while onlookers filmed her; she died of her injuries. She was the third LGBT person killed in Bello that year — the first two were gay men — and the case triggered vigils, protests in several cities and a presidential order to investigate, amid a national tally of 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025 alone.  The national frame around that series, as documented: more than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023 (41 recorded) and eight more between February and April 2024; armed groups in at least one southern department have circulated flyers announcing 'social cleansing' against trans women, in territories where ex-rebel structures persist despite the 2016 peace agreement. The surviving record supports a lethal concentration around Antioquia's metro area — three municipal killings within four months — and documents no province-level protection machinery specific to it.

sources.claim: El País English (14 April 2025), reporting from Bello, Antioquia: 32-year-old trans woman Sara Millerey González Borja was beaten and thrown into a waterway in broad daylight while onlookers filmed; the video went viral on 5 April, President Gustavo Petro ordered an investigation and protests were held in several cities. She was the third LGBTQ person killed in Bello in 2025 (the first two victims were gay men); a clinic reportedly did not treat her as an emergency 'because she didn't get shot', and she died of cardiac arrest the following afternoon. The article records 13 trans people killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025 alone and notes city hall was criticised for using her pre-transition name.

The Guardian (30 July 2024), reporting from Caquetá: more than 40 transgender women were killed in Colombia in 2023 (41 recorded) and eight more between February and April 2024; armed groups circulating in Caquetá - where ex-rebel structures persist despite the 2016 peace agreement - distributed flyers on streets and WhatsApp announcing a 'social cleansing' plan naming 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets, and trans women there were forced to flee after death threats. Retained per rule 5: this supports the record's national-frame claims (2023-24 kill tallies and the southern-department social-cleansing flyers) and no region-specific Antioquia source covers them.

records.name: Hauts-de-France
records.current_summary: The region's documented contact point with trans-visitor risk is prison placement, which national law sets: under criminal-procedure code Article D248 a trans prisoner is held according to the sex on their identity documents, so trans women still marked male are placed in all-male facilities. An investigation published in January 2018 recorded exactly that near the region's principal city: Paola, shouted at and threatened by inmates during three days in a men's facility after a 2014 transfer, and — in the capital — Kara B., held under notorious conditions after a 2016 protest trial; the national detention inspector-general calls transgender detainees the group that suffers most in custody.  The inspector-general's May 2021 opinion, covering every place of deprivation of liberty in the state and built from some forty referrals since 2010, finds serious violations persisting: isolation by reason of trans status, untrained staff, and a 2016 depathologisation law never translated into prison rules. It recommends that detainees choose the sex of searching officers and of their ward, bars identity-based isolation and trans-only wings, and requires continuity of hormone and medical care — recommendations whose non-implementation is itself part of the documented picture for visitors who are detained anywhere in the state, including here.

sources.claim: BuzzFeed investigation posted 12 January 2018: under Article D248 of the criminal-procedure code men and women must be held in separate establishments, but placement follows the legal gender on identity documents, so trans women still recorded as male are held in all-male facilities - the group that, per controller-general Adeline Hazan, 'suffers the most' in prison. Region-relevant case: Paola, transferred in 2014 to Lille's northern correctional facility, was met by detainees shouting 'We don't want any women here!', a fellow inmate tried to attack her with a knife and she spent two days in solitary confinement; Kara B. was held under conditions described as worrying after her 2016 Paris protest trial; the Ministry of Justice counted 13 transgender detainees across eight facilities as of 1 November 2016.

National detention-oversight opinion of 25 May 2021 (covering every place of deprivation of liberty; prepared from referrals received since 2010 concerning transgender detainees): assignment to establishments or wards (male or female) is based exclusively on civil status, so the vast majority of transgender people are held in institutions or wards that do not correspond to their gender identity, and search procedures for persons whose civil-status sex does not match their identity add constraints such as isolation. It recommends guaranteeing every transgender detainee the possibility of choosing the sex of searching officers and of their ward, bars identity-based isolation, requires continuity of medical and hormone care with free choice of doctor, urges research funding, and faults the administration for not translating the 2016 justice-modernisation law (n° 2016-1547 of 18 November 2016) into prison rules.

records.name: Occitanie
records.current_summary: No trans-specific statute, enforcement series or incident record survives in this region's sources; that absence is recorded as absence of documented divergence, not as evidence of local safety. The national framework documented in this record applies unchanged in every commune and department.  That framework is centred on custody. Under criminal-procedure code Article D248 a prisoner is placed by the sex on their identity documents, so trans women still legally marked male are held in all-male facilities; a January 2018 investigation records one such detainee three days in a men's facility near Lille amid inmate threats, and another held in notorious conditions after a 2016 protest trial in the capital. The national detention inspector-general's May 2021 opinion — covering every place of deprivation of liberty, built on some forty referrals since 2010 — finds serious violations persisting: isolation for trans status, untrained staff, and a 2016 depathologisation law never written into prison rules; it recommends that detainees choose the sex of search officers and ward, prohibits identity-based isolation, and requires continuity of medical care, and names transgender detainees as the group that suffers most in the state's custody.

sources.claim: National-framework investigation (BuzzFeed, Rozenn Le Carboulec, published January 2018) on trans women in French prisons — the custody framework the record applies unchanged to this region: Article D248 of the criminal-procedure code places detainees by the sex on their identity documents, so trans women still legally marked male are held in all-male facilities; a trans woman from Argentina whose passport lists her as female spent three days in a men's facility in Lille amid inmate threats (an inmate tried to attack her with a knife), and another detainee was held after a 2016 Paris protest trial; as of 1 November 2016 there were 13 transgender detainees in France, and damages obtained for one detainee's detention conditions were a symbolic 2,000 euros. No Occitanie-specific event appears; the article supports the record's claim that this national custody framework applies in every department.

Opinion of 25 May 2021 by the national detention inspector-general (CGLPL), covering every place of deprivation of liberty and relevant to this region because its visits included the Toulouse-Seysses prison and the Toulouse central police station, with findings concerning eight transgender women held in those Toulouse facilities. Built on referrals received since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons, it documents serious persisting violations — isolation imposed for trans status, staff untrained on trans issues, and the 2016 depathologisation law (n° 2016-1547 of 18 November 2016) never written into prison rules or healthcare guidance — and recommends financing research, policies against discrimination, and suitable procedures for searching and assigning persons whose civil-status sex does not match their presented identity.

records.name: Delhi
records.current_summary: Delhi sits at the centre of the country's 2026 reversal on trans rights: parliament passed an amendment bill removing the right to self-identification, restricting legal recognition to traditionally accepted socio-cultural groups and intersex people, mandating medical certification, and creating new offences of coercion and allurement punishable up to life imprisonment — a de facto reversal of the 2014 constitutional self-determination ruling, cleared by both houses and awaiting presidential assent. The bill triggered rallies in the capital in March 2026, and a supreme-court-appointed advisory panel urged its withdrawal amid privacy and dignity challenges.  The capital is also where the country's trans population is most institutionally visible: the most recent national census recorded 487,803 transgender persons, of whom roughly 32,500 held identity documents — the documentation gap and the protest politics both concentrate here.

sources.claim: National-framework HRW news release, 26 March 2026 — core source for the record's claims: the 2026 Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill removes the right to self-identification, limits legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups and intersex people, mandates medical certification, and creates "coercing or alluring" offences that could criminalise support systems; HRW calls it a major reversal of hard-won rights and urges the president not to sign it. India's last census recorded 487,803 transgender persons but only about 32,500 hold the identity cards essential for social security — the national documentation gap the record concentrates in the capital. No Delhi-specific event in this source.

National-framework BBC News article on the 2026 amendment bill: approved by both houses and now awaiting presidential assent; it removes the right to self-identify in a reversal of the 2014 Supreme Court ruling; the record's capital-protest-politics claim is evidenced here — activist Grace Banu told a press conference in Delhi the community sought "recognition without invasion" and "rights without humiliation" — and a Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel has asked the government to reconsider amid privacy-and-dignity challenges. The government argues the narrower definition will make welfare benefits, job reservations and healthcare support more targeted while strengthening protections against exploitation and trafficking.

records.name: Seoul
records.current_summary: The capital's courts have been the country's clearest rights forum for trans people: a ruling finalised in July 2024 held that police who told a transgender person mid-legal-transition to avoid public restrooms for a while had infringed personal rights, calling comfortable restroom use a fundamental and universal human right and awarding damages. A 2021 national human-rights-commission survey (591 trans respondents) quantified the underlying fear: 41% had used a restroom of another gender out of fear of mistreatment, 39% restricted food and drink to avoid public restrooms, 36% went without; a 2021 district-court judgment awarded damages against a beauty academy that barred a trans student's restroom use.  Recognition has also liberalised judicially: a May 2024 regional decision approved gender-marker change for five trans people without surgery, holding that a surgery requirement violates bodily integrity and reducing the old surgical prerequisites to reference-only status, though some courts still apply them.

sources.claim: Seoul-specific ruling coverage (Korea Times, 22 July 2024): the Seoul Central District Court (presiding judge Chung In-jae) dismissed the state's appeal and ruled partially for plaintiff A in a damages lawsuit against the state, awarding 300,000 won (about $240) of the 3 million won claimed; the decision became final on 2 July 2024 after neither party appealed, holding that a police officer's advice to an LGBT person mid-legal-transition to avoid public restrooms for a while infringed personal rights — "the right to comfortably use restrooms is a fundamental and universal human right." Underpinning data: a 2021 NHRCK survey of 591 trans respondents found 41% used another-gender restrooms out of fear of mistreatment, 39% avoided food and drink, and 36% forwent restroom use altogether; the piece also cites a 2021 Pohang branch of the Daegu District Court ruling of 7 million won damages against an academy that barred a trans student's restroom use.

National judicial-framework item (Yonhap, 8 May 2024): the regional court in the central county of Yeongdong approved male-to-female gender-marker change for five transgender people without sex reassignment surgery, holding it is against the law to determine gender change based on surgery and that every human being has the right to live according to one's gender identity; the national court guidelines that previously required surgery have been downgraded to reference-only status, though some courts still apply them. The ruling is not from a capital court — it evidences the national judicial trend the record cites for Seoul, and no Seoul-specific source covers that claim.

records.name: Selangor
records.current_summary: This state is where the country's religious-enforcement apparatus has been most visibly exercised against gender expression: in 2021 its religious department issued an arrest warrant for a prominent transgender businesswoman over her presentation and mobilised 122 religious-affairs officers in a manhunt that preceded her leaving the country, an episode documented in international analysis of state-backed discrimination against LGBT people in Malaysia.  The national framework applies unchanged here: same-sex conduct is criminalised with sentences up to 20 years and whipping, there is no legal gender recognition, and the day-to-day exposure for gender-nonconforming visitors runs precisely through this state's religious-offence enforcement.

sources.claim: Malaysia country profile (Human Dignity Trust, last updated 16 December 2025) with both the national framework and Selangor-specific enforcement: Penal Code sections 377A-377D criminalise same-sex intimacy and "outrages on decency" with up to twenty years' imprisonment with whipping (a law enforced in recent years; both men and women, and usable against trans people), and Sharia state enactments criminalise cross-dressing and "males posing as females"; Selangor-specific content — the Federal Court struck down provisions of Selangor's Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 as exceeding state power (2021), the Selangor state authorities issued an arrest warrant for a trans businesswoman who failed to appear in court and announced the deployment of 122 religious-affairs officers (the Sajat case), and a Selangor Sharia court sentenced five men to six to seven months' imprisonment with six strokes of the cane; at least 1,733 people had attended state "rehabilitation programmes" as of June 2021, under a crackdown on the LGBT community ongoing since the 2018 election.

HRW/Justice for Sisters report release (10 August 2022) documenting Malaysia's state-backed discrimination, including the Selangor episode the record leads with: in 2021 Nur Sajat, a transgender woman and cosmetics entrepreneur, failed to appear in court in Selangor to answer criminal charges for "insulting Islam" based on her attire; the state's religious department issued a warrant for her arrest and announced it had mobilised 122 religious-affairs officers to hunt her down, then sought her extradition from Thailand — a deployment HRW/JFS cite as showing how far authorities go to enforce rigid gender norms (she was permitted to stay under UNHCR protection and later settled in Australia). National framework context: the federal penal code punishes oral and anal sex with up to 20 years in prison, Sharia codes in the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya criminalise same-sex activity and gender nonconformity, investigations covered Kuala Lumpur, Selangor, Negeri Sembilan, Kelantan, Penang, Pahang and Kedah, and state "rehabilitation" programmes were found to internalise discrimination and foment self-hatred.

records.name: Johor
records.current_summary: Johor operates within the national framework without documented local divergence: same-sex conduct is criminalised with up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping, there is no legal gender recognition, and public-morality offences are enforced through the state's religious authorities — the channel international monitoring documents as driving state-backed discrimination against LGBT people in Malaysia.  No protective or tolerant regime specific to this state is on record. A visitor's exposure here is the national baseline, enforced locally.

sources.claim: Malaysia country profile (Human Dignity Trust, last updated 16 December 2025) — the national-framework source the record's baseline rests on — with Johor-specific content: in November 2023 the Johor government announced plans to establish conversion-therapy centres to "rehabilitate" LGBT people, the record's one documented local divergence beyond the national baseline. The framework applied locally: Penal Code sections 377A-377D criminalise same-sex intimacy and "outrages on decency" with up to twenty years' imprisonment with whipping for both men and women, Sharia enactments prohibit cross-dressing and "males posing as females", same-sex intimacy is also criminalised by state Sharia laws applying to Muslims, and at least 1,733 people had attended "rehabilitation programmes" as of June 2021 under a crackdown ongoing since the 2018 election.

National-framework HRW/Justice for Sisters report release (10 August 2022) supporting the record's claim that the national baseline applies unchanged in Johor and is enforced through state religious authorities: the federal penal code punishes oral and anal sex with up to 20 years in prison, Sharia codes in the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya criminalise same-sex activity and gender nonconformity, state-conducted investigations covered Kuala Lumpur, Selangor, Negeri Sembilan, Kelantan, Penang, Pahang and Kedah, and a crackdown on the LGBT community has run since the 2018 election. No Johor-specific incident appears in this source; the record's local finding (Johor's 2023 conversion-therapy-centre plans) is covered by the paired Human Dignity Trust profile.

records.name: Malacca
records.current_summary: Malacca enforces the national framework with no documented local mitigation: same-sex conduct is criminalised (up to 20 years and whipping), there is no legal gender recognition, and public-morality policing runs through the state's religious authority — the agency type international monitoring identifies as the driver of state-backed discrimination against LGBT people in Malaysia.  The heritage-tourism setting offers no recorded protection; visible gender nonconformity is exposed to that religious enforcement.

sources.claim: National-framework source (applies country-wide, including the state of Malacca): the Human Dignity Trust Malaysia country profile (last updated 2024) reports the Federal Penal Code 1936 ss.377A/377B criminalise same-sex sexual activity with a maximum penalty of twenty years’ imprisonment and whipping, and s.377D “outrages on decency” criminalises gross indecency in terms that can be used to target transgender people; state Sharia enactments additionally criminalise “cross-dressing” for Muslims. It records evidence of the law being enforced in recent years, a crackdown on the LGBT community since the 2018 election, a high-profile 2021 case of a prominent transgender woman fleeing the country following threats of arrest, and consistent reports of discrimination and violence with transgender people particularly vulnerable to physical and verbal abuse.

National-framework source (applies country-wide; no Malacca-specific breakdown): HRW report (published 10 Aug 2022 with Justice for Sisters) documents government-sponsored discrimination against LGBT people in Malaysia, citing the federal penal code punishing oral and anal sex with up to 20 years in prison and Sharia law codes in the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya that typically criminalise same-sex activity and gender nonconformity. It details a hostile official climate — “rehabilitation” and conversion programs, officials shutting down events, and the 2021 prosecution of transgender woman Nur Sajat in western Selangor — and concludes pervasive antipathy toward sexual and gender diversity influences law enforcement, judicial outcomes, family behavior, and public discourse.

records.name: Lima
records.current_summary: Lima concentrates the country's sharpest documented lethality and its newest legal restriction. An LGBTI human-rights observatory at a national university counted 54 LGBTI+ murders for 2020–2023, with trans women the most affected, amid rising hate crimes. In 2025 the national congress — sitting and operating out of the capital — approved a norm against trans people's use of public bathrooms (committee vote February 2025; floor vote April 2025), which a national human-rights institute published an analysis calling legalised discrimination with direct consequences for access to public space.  For a trans visitor, the capital is therefore where both mechanisms bite: the bathroom-restriction norm is national policy administered here, and the murder pattern shows the violence risk when prosecutions are rare and official statistics thin.

sources.claim: National-framework source (binds Lima as national policy): Infobae (20 Feb 2025) reports the Congress Women and Family Commission unanimously approved the Muñante initiative barring trans people from public bathrooms of the sex not matching their biological sex at birth, stating the text also bars “ambiguous” bathroom signage of the kind the international airport Jorge Chávez had placed (“for all persons with female identity” / “male identity”) and that the norm still required plenary backing. LGBTIQ activist Gianna Camacho is quoted calling the measure discriminatory and describing how enforcement would reduce to security staff demanding ID (DNI) based on their own judgment of whether a woman entering is trans.

National-framework source (the norm is national policy, enacted by the congress that sits and operates in Lima): IDEHPUCP analysis (15 Apr 2025, Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte) reports the Congress plenary on Wednesday 2 April 2025 approved, exempt from a second vote, the fused bills 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR; article 5 of the text prohibits entry to and use of public sanitary facilities by any person whose biological sex does not match the sex for which the facility is designated, with listed exceptions. The authors call the rule direct legislation that conditions basic rights on a “biological sex”, a violation of the equality and non-discrimination principle, and note trans people, though framed as aggressors, are more often victims of violence and discrimination.

National-framework source (observatory counts include Lima): Agencia Presentes (22 Jul 2024) reports the TLGBI Rights Observatory annual report recorded 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 reports of rights violations between 2020 and 2023, more than half of the dead being trans women (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian; 2023 saw the most homicides (19) and no suspects were identified in 26 of the 54 killings. It recounts the 12 Feb 2023 kidnapping of transgender sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano (31) from jirón Chancay in central Lima by the “Los Gallegos” extortion gang, who killed her with roughly 30 gunshots, and flags state inaction: no official system records victims’ sexual orientation and hate crimes go unsanctioned.
